strengths: Addresses a challenging and timely problem: multi-subject video generation with identity preservation and semantic alignment.

Proposes a hierarchical identity-preserving attention mechanism with intra-subject, inter-subject, and cross-modal attention; ablation shows removing it drops FaceSim from 58.12 to 51.34, supporting its importance.
Leverages a pretrained VLM for semantic encoding; ablation shows Text-Video Alignment falls from 49.55 to 42.17 without the VLM encoder.
Constructs a large curated dataset and shows via ablation that removing curated data reduces Video Quality from 48.91 to 45.13.
Reports strong quantitative results on identity preservation (FaceSim 60.50, Total Score 57.05) and provides qualitative comparisons against open-source and proprietary baselines.
Demonstrates useful zero-shot applications in controllable video editing, including subject replacement and background modification.
The motivation and related-work discussion clearly situate the work within subject-driven image/video generation and RL-based generative model alignment.
weaknesses: The online RL phase is a central claimed contribution but is critically underspecified: Appendix B.2 'Details of Reward Calculation' is empty; the definitions of R_qual, R_id, and the weights λ_qual, λ_id are not provided. No quantitative ablation isolates the online RL stage; Figure 5 only gives qualitative evidence.

The text/VLM encoder description is inconsistent: the method section states that VLM-enhanced tokens 'replace' the standard text encoder, while the implementation details state a 'dual text-encoder architecture' combining T5 with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. This ambiguity hinders reproducibility and understanding of the architecture.

The claim of 'state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation metrics' is contradicted by Table 1: Ours-14B is not best on Aesthetics (45.00 vs VACE-14B 47.21, Phantom-14B 46.39), GmeScore (67.00 vs Phantom-14B 70.65, VACE-1.3B 71.26, Pika 69.21), or NexusScore (45.00 vs Kling 45.92, Pika 45.41).

The 14B model training is unexplained: the implementation says the model is initialized from Wan-Video-1.3B, but the paper reports Ours-14B results without describing how the 14B variant was obtained, trained, or scaled.
Evaluation is limited to 180 subject-text pairs with no breakdown by number of subjects, so the method's behavior in truly multi-subject settings (e.g., 3+ subjects) is not established.
There is no direct temporal consistency metric; the reported Motion score does not necessarily measure temporal coherence, despite temporal consistency being a central claim.
The Total Score is described as a normalized weighted sum, but the weights are not given, making the headline total-score superiority difficult to verify independently.
No ablation isolates the individual components of the hierarchical attention mechanism (intra-subject vs. inter-subject vs. cross-modal); only the full mechanism is removed.

Architectural details are insufficient for exact reproduction: the attention operations are described only in prose, and it is unclear how latent video tokens participate in each hierarchical stage and how reference images are encoded with a video VAE.
Reproducibility is weakened by missing reward details, undisclosed total-score weights, unexplained 14B training, and reliance on external proprietary image-editing models for dataset curation.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practically relevant problem—multi-subject video generation with identity preservation—that goes beyond the common single-subject setting and has clear applications (personalized content, virtual storytelling, product placement, controllable editing).

The method is a coherent, well-motivated system: hierarchical identity-preserving attention (intra-subject, inter-subject, cross-modal), VLM-based semantic encoding, and an online Flow-GRPO RL stage are integrated sensibly, and the overall pipeline is clearly illustrated (Fig. 2) and described.

Quantitative results (Table 1) are strong: Ours-14B achieves 57.05% Total Score vs 52.32% (Phantom-14B) and 52.87% (VACE-14B), with a large FaceSim gain (60.50% vs 51.48%) and NexusScore gain (45.00% vs 37.43%), which supports the identity-preservation claim. Even the 1.3B variant is competitive with much larger baselines.

The ablation study (Table 2) cleanly isolates each contribution (hierarchical attention, VLM encoder, curated data), showing that removing any component causes consistent degradation, which provides reasonable evidence for the design choices.

The data-curation pipeline (Fig. 3, Appendix C) using VLM-based captioning, Grounding DINO + SAM subject extraction, and Gemini-Flash-Image-based reference synthesis is a substantive engineering contribution, and the paper commits to releasing code, models, and training data, aiding reproducibility.

Qualitative comparisons (Figs. 4–6) are informative and demonstrate the method's ability to preserve multiple identities, maintain temporal coherence, and support zero-shot video editing applications.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: each component (hierarchical/local-global attention, VLM as conditioning encoder, Flow-GRPO-based online RL, data curation with off-the-shelf tools) builds on prior work cited by the authors, and the paper's contribution is primarily their combination plus engineering, rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Evaluation breadth is limited: only 180 subject-text pairs are used, and the Total Score is a self-defined normalized weighted sum of other metrics, which makes the headline 'state-of-the-art' claim partly dependent on an arbitrary aggregation. Absolute comparisons on individual metrics are more informative.

Metric design deserves more scrutiny: FaceSim and NexusScore emphasize face/subject similarity; it is unclear how these are computed for non-human subjects (e.g., objects, animals), and the NaturalScore relies on an MLLM's judgment, which may introduce bias. Reporting correlations with human judgment would strengthen the claims.

No human/user study is reported, which is a notable omission for a generation task where perceptual quality and identity fidelity are central; automated metrics alone may not fully capture subject consistency and prompt alignment.

Implementation details for the hierarchical attention are underspecified: how the subject tokens are injected into the DiT backbone (e.g., at which layers, how temporal consistency is maintained for subject tokens, memory/compute overhead of the extra attention stages) is not fully described, which limits reproducibility and understanding of the design's generality.

Training/RL costs are not quantified. The online RL stage with Flow-GRPO typically requires many rollouts; the paper does not report the wall-clock cost, GPU hours for RL, or how sensitive results are to reward weights (λ_qual, λ_id), which are important for assessing practicality.

The paper claims the method 'outperforms existing methods' but some baselines (e.g., certain proprietary systems) are only compared qualitatively, and a few recent concurrent works (e.g., PolyVivid, VideoMage, FantasyPortrait) are discussed but not quantitatively compared in Table 1, leaving the relative standing on multi-subject scenarios somewhat incomplete.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and practically relevant problem — multi-subject video generation with identity preservation from text plus multiple reference images — and frames the three sub-challenges (identity, semantic integration, temporal consistency) clearly in the introduction.

The core architectural idea is simple but sensible: factorizing attention into intra-subject, inter-subject, and cross-modal stages. The ablation in Table 2 shows this is not cosmetic — FaceSim drops from 58.12% to 51.34% when replaced by flat concatenation, which is a large and credible effect.

The VLM-based conditioning is also supported by the ablation: Text-Video Alignment falls from 49.55% to 42.17% when the VLM is removed, consistent with the claim that stronger semantic encoding helps compositional prompts.

The data-curation pipeline (motion/aesthetics filtering, VLM captioning and subject naming, Grounding DINO + SAM masking, editing-model-based subject synthesis) is a reasonable engineering contribution, and the paper does report dataset statistics (Figs. 7-8) rather than only asserting the dataset exists.
The zero-shot controllable video editing demonstration (Fig. 6, Sec. 4.4) is an appealing downstream application that follows naturally from the architecture.
Writing is generally clear, related work is thorough, and the hierarchical/RL/VLM combination is described at a readable level.
weaknesses: The headline claim of state-of-the-art performance is not supported by the authors' own table. Sec. 4.2 states the model achieves SOTA 'across all evaluation metrics,' yet Table 1 shows Ours-14B underperforming Phantom-14B on Aesthetics (45.00 vs 46.67) and Motion (40.00 vs 46.67), and Ours-1.3B's Total (54.33) is below Kling 1.6 (54.46). The win is concentrated in FaceSim and NexusScore.

The headline 'Total Score' is a self-defined normalized weighted sum whose weights are never given ('Further details are provided in Appendix D,' but Appendix D only defines NexusScore, NaturalScore, and GmeScore, not the weighting). Since the composite metric carries the main comparative claim, this makes the central quantitative result unverifiable and potentially tuned toward the metrics the method targets.

The architecture description is internally inconsistent, which materially undermines reproducibility. Sec. 3.2.1 states that VLM-enhanced tokens 'replace the embeddings from a standard text encoder' with C_ctx = [f_txt; f_1; ...; f_N], whereas Sec. 4.1 says 'we employ a dual text-encoder architecture, combining T5 with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct.' These two statements cannot both be true, and the paper never explains how 7B-scale Qwen2.5-VL hidden states (different tokenizer, different dimensionality) are projected/aligned into the MMDiT cross-attention space.

It is also unclear which model is actually trained and evaluated. Sec. 3.2.1 describes the DiT as 'a substantial 14B parameter transformer,' Table 3 lists both 1.3B and 14B MMDiT variants, Table 1 reports both, but Sec. 4.1 says the model is 'initialized from the weights of the Wan-Video-1.3B model' and the entire ablation (Table 2) matches the 1.3B numbers. The 14B variant receives no ablation or training description.

Key method details are missing, including at least one appendix section that is literally empty: 'B.2 DETAILS OF REWARD CALCULATION' appears as a bare heading with no content before Section C. The reward R_total = lambda_qual R_qual + lambda_id R_id is defined only symbolically: R_qual and R_id are never operationalized, and lambda values are never given. The online RL contribution therefore cannot be assessed or reproduced, and there is no ablation isolating the RL stage in Table 2 despite it being listed as one of the three main contributions.

The evaluation is narrow relative to the claims. Only 180 subject-text pairs are used; there is no user study; there is no analysis of how identity/temporal quality degrades as the number of subjects grows (2 vs 3+); and there is no failure-case analysis for occlusion, interaction, or subject overlap, even though 'complex interactions between multiple subjects' is a stated motivation. Related multi-subject methods explicitly discussed in Sec. 2 (VideoMage, PolyVivid, CINEMA, Concat-ID) are not included in Table 1.

Two of the five reported metrics (NaturalScore via MLLM judgment, GmeScore via Qwen2-VL text/video embeddings) are themselves model-based and unvalidated; the paper provides no correlation analysis against human judgment, so improvements on these axes are weak evidence. NexusScore and FaceSim both depend on Grounded-SAM masking quality, another unquantified confound.

Technical novelty is incremental. Hierarchical attention is a three-stage factorization of standard self-attention; the VLM encoder is an off-the-shelf Qwen2.5-VL used as a conditioner; the RL stage is Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025a) with a task-specific reward. Each piece is a recombination of existing components, and the paper does not provide analysis (e.g., attention visualization, perplexity measurements) to substantiate the claimed mechanism of 'higher perplexity during semantic integration and conflict resolution' that the design is supposedly fixing.

The dataset contribution is difficult to verify or reuse: it depends on proprietary tools (Gemini-Flash-Image) and on OpenS2V-Nexus derivatives, yet the abstract promises 'training data will be released' without addressing licensing, and there is no ethics/consent discussion for an identity-preserving face-and-person video generator — a notable omission given the obvious misuse surface.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem — compositional multi-subject video generation with both identity preservation and temporal coherence — which is under-explored relative to single-subject video customization.

The proposed framework thoughtfully integrates three complementary components: a hierarchical identity-preserving attention mechanism (intra-subject, inter-subject, cross-modal stages), VLM-based semantic grounding via Qwen2.5-VL, and an online RL (Flow-GRPO) post-training stage with a composite fidelity/quality reward.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: quantitative comparison against open-source (VACE, Phantom, SkyReels-A2) and proprietary (Vidu, Pika, Kling) systems, ablations of the hierarchical attention (Table 2, Table S.5), VLM encoder, data curation, RL algorithm (DPO vs. GRPO), and individual reward terms (Table 3, Table S.7).
The human preference study (30 participants, 200 comparisons, Fig. S.13) is a valuable complement to automated metrics and partially addresses concerns about metric circularity and reward hacking.
The data curation pipeline is described in detail with dataset statistics (Tables S.4, S.8; Figs. S.9–S.12), which aids understanding of the training regime and is a practical contribution.

The analysis of the reward ablation is honest — the authors explicitly note the reward-hacking scenario when the naturalness reward is removed (increased FaceSim/Aesthetics but degraded Q-Align), rather than glossing over it.
Reported gains over strong baselines (e.g., FaceSim 60.71% for the 14B model vs. 48.55% for Phantom-14B) are substantial across multiple metrics, supporting the central claims.
weaknesses: The individual components are largely existing techniques (cross-attention designs, VLM encoders, Flow-GRPO); the primary novelty is their combination and application to multi-subject video generation, which limits the algorithmic originality.

Evaluation partly relies on metrics tied to the same benchmark the authors claim ("NexusScore, a metric from our proposed OpenS2V-Eval benchmark"), which raises concerns about independence and self-referential evaluation, even though the underlying benchmark is cited as a separate work.

The comparison with proprietary systems (Vidu, Pika, Kling) may not be entirely fair, as these models are not necessarily designed or conditioned for multi-subject identity preservation; the resulting margins should be interpreted cautiously.

The labeling of "Ours-1.3B (Base Model)" is misleading — this variant already includes the hierarchical attention, VLM encoder, and curated dataset, and it already surpasses 14B open-source baselines by large margins. This makes it difficult to attribute gains cleanly, and suggests the dataset/architecture dominates over the RL contribution.

Dataset curation depends on proprietary tools (Nano Banana/Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, QwenVL-72B), which limits reproducibility even if the curated dataset is released, and could bias the training distribution toward artifacts of those tools.

Presentation issues: typos (e.g., "determinsistic"), and Equation 4 (stochastic noise injection) is not clearly derived or justified, making the transition from deterministic flow matching to the stochastic RL rollout hard to verify.
Evaluation breadth is limited to 180 subject-text pairs, and no quantitative efficiency comparison (training/inference cost vs. baselines) is reported, despite the added RL stage and VLM overhead.

Ablations show the "base model" already achieves SOTA-level results, so the marginal contribution of online RL (a key claimed novelty) is comparatively small relative to the architecture/data pipeline, weakening the emphasis placed on RL in the framing.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: compositional multi-subject video generation with identity preservation, semantic alignment, and temporal coherence.
Proposes a coherent framework that integrates hierarchical identity-preserving attention, VLM-based semantic guidance, and online RL (Flow-GRPO) into a video diffusion backbone.
Provides strong quantitative results on the OpenS2V-Nexus benchmark, outperforming or matching open-source and proprietary baselines on key metrics such as FaceSim, NexusScore, and total score.
Includes extensive ablations isolating the contributions of hierarchical attention, VLM semantic encoding, curated training data, and online RL with different reward components.
Reports a human preference study (30 participants, 200 questionnaires) that supports the automatic metrics, especially for identity consistency and motion naturalness.
Supplementary material is detailed, with architecture configurations, RL hyperparameters, reward design, dataset composition statistics, and additional qualitative results.
Demonstrates practical downstream utility through zero-shot controllable video editing and multi-subject scene composition.
Overall writing is clear and the method is well motivated, with a useful problem formulation and strong empirical evidence.
weaknesses: The introduction claims a 'contrastive learning mechanism' as a contribution, but no such mechanism is described in the method or supplementary material. This is a significant unsupported claim.
The 'Video Quality' metric in Table 2 is not defined, and the paper uses inconsistent metric names across tables (e.g., Aesthetics vs. Video Quality), making some comparisons hard to interpret.

The claim of pioneering online RL for multi-subject video generation is weakened by related work Identity-GRPO [33], which already applies RL to multi-human identity-preserving video generation; the novelty should be positioned more carefully.

Reproducibility is limited by the dataset curation pipeline: it relies on internal high-quality videos and synthetic data generated by proprietary image editing models (e.g., Nano Banana), which may not be publicly available or stable over time.

Evaluation protocol details are incomplete: it is unclear whether the 180 subject-text pairs are a public held-out split of OpenS2V-Nexus or a newly constructed set, and baseline generation settings for proprietary models are not specified.

Main quantitative results and the human preference study lack error bars or statistical significance tests, and the human study provides minimal details on participant demographics, randomization, or significance.

The reward design uses automated metrics (FaceSim, NexusScore, Aesthetic, NaturalScore) that may be imperfect and potentially hackable; although NaturalScore is introduced to mitigate this, the extent of reward hacking is not fully quantified.
Training details for the 14B model are unclear—specifically whether it uses the full proposed method and online RL—making the scaling comparison and SOTA claim less transparent.
Some supplementary sections are incomplete (e.g., D.1 Evaluation on Multi-Subject Scenarios appears only as a title), and minor typos/repetitions reduce clarity.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem — compositional multi-subject video generation with identity preservation — that has clear practical value for controllable content creation.

The proposed framework integrates several components (hierarchical ID-preserving attention, VLM semantic grounding, online GRPO post-training) in a coherent pipeline, and the ablation studies (Table 2, Table S.5) credibly attribute gains to each stage, notably showing the cross-modal attention (Stage 3) is the most critical.
Reports both automated metrics and a human preference study (Fig. S.13), which partially mitigates the reliance on the authors' own automatic metrics.
Includes a detailed data-curation pipeline (Fig. S.8) with statistics (Table S.8, Figs. S.9–S.10) and a comparison of reference-image construction strategies (Fig. S.11), which adds practical value.
Shows improvements over strong open-source baselines (Phantom-1.3B/14B, VACE, SkyReels-A2) and provides an in-depth discussion of GRPO stability and reward design in the supplement.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: hierarchical attention, VLM conditioning, and GRPO-style online RL for diffusion models all exist in prior work (e.g., Flow-GRPO [28], Dance-GRPO [62], ID-GRPO [33]). The contribution is essentially an engineering combination rather than a fundamentally new method; the claim of being the first to apply online RL to multi-subject video generation is narrow.

The central 'state-of-the-art' claim is not convincingly supported by Table 1. Against the proprietary Kling 1.6, the 14B model wins only on FaceSim (60.71 vs 40.10) and GmeScore, while losing on Aesthetics (45.28 vs 44.60), Motion (40.34 vs 41.60), NexusScore (45.11 vs 45.92), and NaturalScore (73.23 vs 79.06). The overall 'Total Score' advantage appears to be driven almost entirely by FaceSim, suggesting the aggregate metric is weighted toward the property the method is designed to optimize.

The Total Score is defined only as 'a normalized weighted sum of other scores' with no disclosure of the weights or normalization. This makes the headline ordering in Table 1 non-reproducible and raises concerns that the aggregate metric is tailored to favor identity preservation. This is a material evaluation issue.

NexusScore and NaturalScore are adopted from the OpenS2V-Nexus benchmark [68], which appears closely related to the authors' group. Using these metrics as the primary evidence of superiority without independent validation risks circular evaluation; the paper does not report standard, widely-accepted baselines such as standard VBench or CLIP-based alignment as primary evidence.

Motion quality is not improved (or is worse than Kling 1.6), yet the abstract and introduction frame the method as harmonizing 'identity consistency with motion quality.' This claim is not well supported by the numbers presented.

Data curation depends on proprietary models (Nano Banana / Gemini 2.5 Flash Image [11]) for reference image construction. This undermines reproducibility and makes it unclear how much of the reported gain stems from a proprietary data engine rather than the proposed architecture or RL.

Ablation evidence for the reward design is mixed: Table 3 shows that removing the Natural reward actually increases FaceSim and Aesthetics while only degrading Q-Align, which weakens the argument that the multi-faceted reward robustly mitigates reward hacking. The claimed benefits of the online RL stage are modest (Total Score 54.33 → 55.16, ~1.5% relative).

The writing contains numerous typos and grammatical errors (e.g., 'While convert flow matching's deterministic generation process', 'Table ??' in Sec. 4.3), which harms clarity and suggests insufficient proofreading. The manuscript also introduces new metrics (NexusScore, NaturalScore) without fully motivating why existing community metrics are insufficient.

The 1.3B base model (54.33) already matches or exceeds Kling 1.6 (54.46 vs. ~54.3), which raises questions about whether the benchmark setup and metric weighting are appropriately calibrated to reflect real perceptual quality; the qualitative examples (Fig. 4) are hard to verify from sparse frames alone.
